Each words in the file will become an argument to echo, discarding newlines, spaces, tabs, etc (but including a single space between each words).

echo returns a single line when you do not use double quotes.

sakuramboo@Betsy:~$ echo `cat Input.txt`
one two three
sakuramboo@Betsy:~$ echo "`cat Input.txt`"
one
two
three
There looks to be some better solutions with sed and tr

In bash any whitespace is used to seperate atoms of text into arguments and echo will print each argument with a space delimiter. I wish I had thought of that trick.

This is the same as doing sed 's/\s\+/ /g'

This takes any segment of one or more characters of whitespace, of any kind, and replaces it with a space.

Edit: Not quite because sed evaluates line by line. This is almost fixed by -z which processes the whole thing as one line. Nearly fixes except that sed doesn't see newline as a whitespace character but bash does.
